Chapter 7: The Unity Principle — Harnessing Shared Identity.
You know, as we build on the power of association, there’s another level that really brings people together—it's called the principle of unity. This is all about that deep sense of shared identity or belonging, the kind of thing that makes you feel like you’re part of something bigger. When folks see themselves as part of a group, a family, or a community, they're so much more open to being influenced by those they see as “one of us.”
But here’s the thing—unity isn’t about just having surface-level similarities. It’s about creating a real, authentic connection. That connection might come from shared experiences, common values, working toward the same goals, or even facing the same challenges. That feeling of “we’re in this together” lays down a foundation of trust and cooperation, making persuasion not just easier, but longer-lasting.
So, how do you actually build unity with the people around you? Here are a few ways you can get started:
First, highlight common ground. When you kick off a conversation or a project, try pointing out what you all share—maybe it’s a similar experience, a value you all care about, or a big goal you’re chasing together.
Next, use inclusive language. Simple words like “we,” “us,” and “together” can work wonders. They help everyone feel like they belong and that you’re all partners in this.
And don’t forget the power of shared experiences. Getting involved in group activities or little rituals can build that sense of identity and mutual support.
Imagine a leader rolling out a new initiative—if they start by reminding the team of a tough moment everyone got through together, that shared memory becomes more than just a story. It’s a touchstone, a reminder of the team’s strength and resilience.
Unity really shines when trust is shaky or there’s a lot of resistance. If people feel seen, included, and valued, they’re much more likely to listen, work together, and welcome new ideas. That’s why unity is at the heart of great community organizing, strong teams, and even close families.
And here’s something to remember—unity doesn’t always need to come from grand gestures. Sometimes, it’s the small things—a kind word, a moment of empathy, or simply acknowledging someone’s effort—that make a real difference. It’s all about moving away from that “us versus them” mindset, and choosing to build a true spirit of partnership.
